newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW - Financial market comments.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW - Financial market comments.

text.p: Following are comments by economists and other financial markets players after first round French parliamentary election polling closed at 1800 GMT and all opinion polling institutes predicted the left leading.
DARREN WILLIAMS, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST, UBS:
I thought the left would do better than some were predicting but I must admit that this is beyond my expectations. It'll liven things up in the market tomorrow.
It's difficult with the markets because they've been so complacent. They can either be complacent again or take it pretty hard. I suspect they'll take it pretty hard.
If the Socialists win at the end of the day the differences will only be on the fringes but that's not the question for tomorrow. The U.S. and UK markets being closed may mute things a little though.
MARIE OWENS-THOMSEN, ECONOMIST, BIP:
It's pretty as much as bad as it could get but we don't know who will win the second round. The markets would rather not have seen the left and the National Front achieving this performance.
What does this mean for the markets? it is difficult to say. The stock market risks selling off more than the bond market. The bond market sold off quite significantly on Thursday and Friday.
There may be a knee-jerk reaction. But in the last parliamentary election...we had a similar situation.

The left did well in the first round and the the right caught up in the second round. I do not expect them to clean up in the second round. But this type of a first round result might bring out more people to the voting urns. There is a high probability that second round will not look the first round.
PHILIPPE BROSSARD, HEAD OF RESEARCH, ABN AMRO FINANCE:
It's a big surprise. The franc is weakening and obviously the markets should open much lower tomorrow morning.

It could be negative for the lira and the peseta as well - seen as negative for convergence trades if the Socialists got a victory. Although at the end of the campaign they were a bit softer on Europe they sounded if they were coming back to a more centrist line.

Obviously unless something changes between the two rounds the left may win. It's definitely a mistake of the opinion polls first of all. High abstentions mean there will be a lower number of candidates for the far right in the second round.

I see Pibor (June interest rate future) off 10 basis points at least. 96.38 would be a good level but it may be a touch lower. The 10-year spread (between the French OAT and German Bund) at minus eight or minus six basis points (from -14 now) and the two-year spread widening by about eight basis points.
ELISABETTA CASTELLI, HEAD INTERNATIONAL EQUITY SALES, CDC:
This is definitely bad news for the (stock) market. We could see a two percent correction tomorrow, but I would be surprised if it was more.

The left has not so far shown it has a credible programme and it has not embraced market economics in the way the current U.K. government has. It is talking about undoing privatisations, it poses a question over Maastricht. This is a setback for corporate governance in France.
It depends what the left says in the coming week, whether they backtrack.
HERVE GOULLETQUER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CREDIT LYONNAIS:
"It'll probably be choppy in the stock and bond markets tomorrow, but not too rough. Markets will digest the fact that the left could win and this will lead to a fall.

But the markets will above all turn their attention to the left this week to see if they continue to adopt a pragmatic and modern approach, as they were doing late in the campaign, or if they will go for the more traditional, social style of earlier in the campaign.
If they stick to the pragmatic style the markets should not unravel too much. On Monday the stock market is likely to fall more than the bond market.
JACQUES CHAHINE, HEAD OF JACQUES CHAHINE MARKET CONSULTANCY:
It's a bit of a disappointment for the right. I can see people taking some precautions tomorrow and I wouldn't be surprised to see the market (CAC-40 leading share index) fall three to four percent.
OLIVIER BLITZ, EQUITIES TRADER, IFF BOURSE:

I'm not very optimistic for the stock market tomorrow. Few were expecting (election) figures like these. I'd expect a (CAC-40) fall of at least two percent at the open and it could be more if volumes are thin.
IAIN LINDSAY, SENIOR BOND ANALYST, CREDIT LYONNAIS

It's quite a remarkable and interesting result. It's defintely a backfire for Chriac, even if Chirac can catch up a bit it's so close to the wire. For the ploy to have worked he would need a majority of 50-plus seats.

The 10-year (bond) spread (over Germany) could be knocked into single digits (from minus 14 now), but I'm not convinced it will be hit too badly. I think there will be a relatively low key reaction although the curve will flatten.

(June) PIBOR could lose 20 centimes or maybe more. The franc will depend on the will and the purchasing power of the Bank of France to hold it in check. Certainly if it got above 3.38 and targetted 3.40, PIBOR would get hit badly. PIBOR moves will probably be ahead of the currency if (the franc) is being articficially supported.
-- Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
